nameStory: The name "chokecherry" comes from the astringent, puckering quality of the raw fruit that literally makes you choke when you bite into it. The scientific name "virginiana" refers to the Virginia colony, where early European botanists first described this native North American species. Despite the choking sensation, Indigenous peoples and early settlers learned to process these cherries into jellies and pemmican once they discovered cooking mellows the harsh tannins.
description: Chokecherry is a small native tree or large shrub that typically grows 6-20 feet tall, forming dense thickets through root sprouting. In late spring, it produces showy white flower clusters that look like fluffy bottlebrushes standing upright on the branches. The dark red to nearly black cherries that follow are about the size of a pea and hang in drooping clusters. This hardy member of the rose family is one of our most widespread native cherries, thriving in a variety of conditions across New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, upright cylindrical clusters of small white flowers, 3-6 inches long, that smell sweetly fragrant and attract clouds of bees and butterflies in late May to early June

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with finely toothed edges that feel smooth and somewhat thick; arranged alternately on branches and turn yellow to reddish in fall

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small dark red to black cherries in drooping clusters that taste extremely astringent and bitter when raw, ripening in late summer and often persisting into fall

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on young stems that develops shallow furrows with age; when scratched, inner bark has a distinctive bitter almond scent

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows in dense colonies or thickets from spreading roots, with multiple stems arising from the base; can be shrubby or form a small single-trunked tree

habitat: Chokecherry thrives in forest edges, clearings, stream banks, and disturbed soils throughout New England from sea level to mountain slopes. It's particularly common along hiking trails, old roads, and forest borders where it gets partial to full sun. You'll often find it growing alongside elderberry, dogwoods, and other edge-loving shrubs in both acidic and alkaline soils.

seasonality.spring: Spectacular white bottlebrush flower clusters appear in late May to early June, filling the air with sweet fragrance and buzzing with pollinators. New leaves emerge bright green and soft.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small green cherries develop, gradually darkening to red then nearly black by late summer. Leaves are at their fullest and darkest green.
seasonality.fall: Ripe dark cherries hang in drooping clusters while leaves turn yellow to orange-red before dropping. Fruit often persists after leaf fall, providing food for birds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the smooth grayish bark and alternate bud arrangement. Old fruit clusters may still cling to branches, and the tendency to grow in thickets becomes obvious.

funFact: Despite tasting terrible raw, chokecherries contain more antioxidants than blueberries and were a crucial survival food for Indigenous peoples and pioneers who learned to dry and pound them into nutritious pemmican - the tannins that make them astringent actually help preserve the mixture for months without refrigeration.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with black cherry, but chokecherry's flowers grow in upright bottlebrush clusters while black cherry flowers hang in drooping clusters. Remember: chokecherry flowers "stand up" like they're choking, while black cherry flowers "hang down" in shame.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name scare you - while the raw fruit is astringent, chokecherries are not poisonous like some other plants with "choke" in the name. However, like other cherry species, the leaves, bark, and pits contain compounds that can be toxic if consumed in large quantities, especially when wilted.
compareHints: Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets. Black cherry grows much larger as a forest tree with drooping flower clusters, while fire cherry is smaller with flowers in small rounded clusters. Beach plum is coastal only and has much rounder, plum-like fruits rather than small cherries.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
